h1:
Sisaket With Kids
Million Bottle Temple, Huai Nam Kham, Durian, Cafes
intro: Sisaket is an easier place to travel with kids than most people expect. The main sights in town are clustered close together, and they include an aquarium with a fish tunnel that kids love, an island in the middle of a reservoir where they can run around and cycle, and the Million Bottle Temple, which kids enjoy for the bright colors. During durian season (June–August) you can also head up to the volcanic-soil orchards and eat fresh fruit right in the grove. This trip is built for a family with kids over 2-3 days, keeping an unhurried pace with somewhere shaded for every hot afternoon, complete with times, real entry fees, and food spots where you can actually sit down with kids.

blocks.html: Traveling with kids means pacing things well — one minute they're hot, the next hungry, the next sleepy. The good thing about Sisaket is that the family-friendly sights in town all sit close together, just a few minutes' drive apart. The volcanic durian orchards and waterfalls are down south around Khun Han and Kantharalak, about 1–1.5 hours from town. So we set the first day for sights in town to let the kids settle in, then head south the next day. This plan keeps somewhere shaded for every afternoon, because the Isan sun is genuinely strong — keeping kids out in the midday heat for long just isn't worth it.

blocks.title: Getting there, and the easiest way with kids
blocks.html: From Bangkok you can take the Lower Isan train line straight to Sisaket station — for small kids, a sleeper train is more comfortable than a coach. If you fly, land at Ubon Ratchathani airport and continue to town by road, about 1.5 hours. Once you reach town, the family-friendly sights are mostly concentrated in the city, but if you want to head south to the durian orchards or waterfalls, public transport is very limited. I'd rent a car and drive yourself — it's far more flexible with kids, you can fit a car seat, and stop for the bathroom whenever your little one needs it.

If you have two days, this layout fits a kid's pace nicely. Spend the first day entirely in town, focused on the aquarium and the island where kids can play for a long stretch. On the second day head south, stopping at the Million Bottle Temple, the volcanic durian orchards (durian season only), then wrap up at a cafe before heading back.

blocks.label: Day 1
blocks.title: In town — Huai Nam Kham island + Sisaket Aquarium

items.activity: Start at Huai Nam Kham island (80th Anniversary Commemorative Park)
items.note: An island in the middle of a reservoir in town, in Nong Khrok subdistrict, with a shaded public park, walking paths and a cycling track around the island. Kids can run around freely, and the morning sun is still gentle — a good spot to let them burn off some energy first.

items.activity: Enter Sisaket Aquarium (aquatic life center) on the island
items.note: The highlight for kids is the underwater glass tunnel, about 24 meters long — you walk through with fish swimming around your head. There are over 4,000 freshwater and saltwater fish. Open Tuesday–Sunday, 10:00–16:00 (closed Monday). Entry is 30 THB for adults, 20 THB for kids; children under 100 cm tall and seniors enter free. It's a cool, air-conditioned spot for the late morning.

items.activity: (Daily at 14:00) Watch the diver fish-feeding show in the big tank
items.note: Every day at 2pm there's a diving show where staff feed the fish — kids love it. If you want to catch it, time your lunch and sightseeing so you're back for this slot. At certain times there's also a koi-feeding activity with milk bottles that little kids find fun.

items.activity: Lunch in town, at a spot that's easy with kids
items.note: In town there are plenty of made-to-order shops, noodle places and Isan restaurants. You can order non-spicy dishes for kids — fried rice, omelette, fried tilapia. Prices run from a few dozen baht to a little over a hundred per plate.

items.activity: Cafe break in town, out of the heat
items.note: There are several relaxed cafes in town, such as Lhong Pah Cafe, a leafy garden cafe with photo corners and space for kids to wander, open around 09:00–20:00. Or Cafe De Tree, which has a food zone and a rooftop. Coffee and drinks run about 50–90 THB a glass, with milk drinks and snacks for kids.

items.activity: Dinner and a stroll through the evening market in town
items.note: The evening market in town has plenty of cheap local food — grilled items, sticky rice, sweets — so kids can pick and try a few things. Save your energy for heading south tomorrow.

blocks.label: Day 2
blocks.title: South to Khun Han — Million Bottle Temple + volcanic durian orchards

items.activity: Leave town and drive south to Khun Han district
items.note: It's about 60 km and takes roughly 1–1.5 hours. The later part of the drive runs past rice fields and green hills. Plan a gas-station bathroom break along the way for the kids, and fill the tank before heading south, since stations get sparse out there.

items.activity: Million Bottle Temple (Wat Pa Maha Chedi Kaew), Non Sung subdistrict, Khun Han district
items.note: A temple decorated with over 1.5 million colored glass bottles — from the entrance gate to the ordination hall, the pavilions, and even the bathrooms. Kids love it for the bold colors and the sheer oddity of it. The highlight is the cruciform ordination hall set over water. Open around 08:00–17:00, free entry. Dress modestly in the hall area, and keep a close eye on kids near the water.

items.activity: (Durian season, Jun–Aug) Stop at a volcanic durian orchard around Khun Han–Bak Dong
items.note: Volcanic durian is grown on reddish-brown volcanic soil — the flesh is sweet and rich with a less pungent smell. Many orchards let you sit and eat in the grove, and there are also rambutan and mangosteen for kids. Prices at the orchard run about 180–250 THB/kg depending on grade. It gets busy at peak around late June, so you can book an orchard ahead. Out of season (Sep–May) most orchards close — swap in a waterfall or cafe instead.

The district has Isan restaurants and made-to-order shops. Try fried tilapia with sweet fish sauce, grilled chicken and sticky rice. You can order non-spicy dishes for kids, and the prices are gentle.

items.activity: Cafe in the fields around Khun Han–Kantharalak, out of the heat
items.note: The south has several cafes with rice-field and mountain views — shady, with plenty of open space for kids to wander. It's a good place to rest during the strong afternoon sun before the drive back. Coffee runs about 50–80 THB a glass, with cold drinks and snacks for kids.

Southern souvenirs include volcanic durian (in season), rambutan, orchard mangosteen, volcanic-soil dyed fabric, and Thung Kula jasmine rice — all available in town. Allow about 1–1.5 hours for the drive back into the city.

blocks.title: Book the activities in your Sisaket trip ahead
blocks.text: Booking online ahead on Klook or GetYourGuide is usually cheaper than the gate and skips the queue. Pick only the experiences you actually want — prices and availability are shown live on each site.

items.label: Day trips from Sisaket
items.note: Out and back in a day

blocks.text: With 3 days, what else can you add for the kids

blocks.html: If you have three days, there's no need to cram everything into two. Add an easy day for in-town spots where kids can play for a while, plus a temple with a museum where kids can see real artifacts — so neither the kids nor the adults end up worn out.

blocks.label: Extra day
blocks.title: An easy day in town — Phra That Rueang Rong + water park

items.activity: Wat Phra That Rueang Rong, a stupa blending four ethnic styles
items.note: A six-tier stupa whose lower floor is a folk museum telling the way of life of the Lao, Khmer, Suay and Yer peoples, with real artifacts for kids to see. Head to the upper floors for city views. Free entry, a short walk — a nice gentle morning with kids.

items.activity: Splash around at Sabaidee Water Park
items.note: A water park in the province where kids can play all day, with slides and a kids' pool. Check opening times and entry fees with the venue's page before going, as they vary by season. Bring your own swimwear and towels — this is usually the kids' favorite day of the trip.

items.activity: Back to a cafe in town to rest before dinner
items.note: After all the swimming, find a chill cafe in town — order iced milk and snacks for the kids while the adults sip coffee, before closing the trip with dinner in town.

blocks.text: Family-friendly spots where kids can play for a while

blocks.html: If you'd rather pick your own days and destinations, below are the spots where kids stay happy the longest, ranked by how well they suit kids. Mix and match them into your plan based on your child's age and interests.

items.name: Sisaket Aquarium
items.blurb: An aquatic life center on Huai Nam Kham island, with a roughly 24-meter underwater glass tunnel and over 4,000 fish, plus a diver fish-feeding show at 2pm. Open Tuesday–Sunday, 10:00–16:00. Adults 30, kids 20 THB.

items.name: Huai Nam Kham island
items.blurb: A public park on an island in a reservoir in town, with a cycling track and open ground for kids to run around, and plenty of shade. Go in the morning or evening when the sun is gentle. Free entry.

items.name: Million Bottle Temple (Wat Pa Maha Chedi Kaew)
items.blurb: A forest temple in Khun Han decorated with over 1.5 million glass bottles — bold colors and fun for photos. The highlight is the cruciform ordination hall over water. Open 08:00–17:00, free entry.

items.name: Volcanic durian orchards (durian season)
items.blurb: From June–August, many orchards around Khun Han–Bak Dong let you sit and eat durian, rambutan and mangosteen in the grove, and kids get to see fruit on the tree. About 180–250 THB/kg at the orchard.

blocks.text: What to eat when traveling Sisaket with kids

blocks.html: A lot of Isan food is spicy and bold, so you have to choose carefully with kids. Below are dishes and types of places that work for sitting down with kids — non-spicy options for the little ones, local specialties for the adults, and cafes with drinks and snacks for kids too. They're ordered from easiest to hardest to manage with kids.

items.name: Fried tilapia with sweet fish sauce
items.blurb: Sisaket is known for farm-raised tilapia — fried crisp and topped with sweet fish sauce. The fish is sweet and not spicy, easy for kids, eaten with steamed or sticky rice. Local shops in town and Khun Han do it well.

items.name: Volcanic durian (seasonal)
items.blurb: The southern star, grown on volcanic soil around Khun Han–Kantharalak. The flesh is sweet and rich with a less pungent smell, and kids who can handle durian will like it for the soft, sweet texture. Available from the tree June–August.

items.name: Grilled chicken & sticky rice
items.blurb: An easy dish for kids — fragrant grilled chicken pulled apart and eaten with hot sticky rice, found all over town and across the districts. Order som tam alongside for the adults, while the kids stick to chicken and sticky rice.

items.name: Volcanic-orchard rambutan & mangosteen (seasonal)
items.blurb: Same window as durian — orchards around Kantharalak–Khun Han have fresh rambutan and mangosteen, picked sweet and juicy. Kids love them because they're easy to eat with no cooking, and they make good souvenirs to take home.

items.name: Noodles & rice porridge in town
items.blurb: On days when kids don't want anything bold, the noodle and rice-porridge shops in town are a safe fallback — mild broth kids can sip, filling and quick. Found all over town.

items.name: Lhong Pah Cafe
items.blurb: A leafy garden cafe with lots of trees, photo corners and space for kids to wander. Coffee, cold drinks and bakery items. Open around 09:00–20:00 — a good spot to rest during the hot afternoon.

items.name: Cafe De Tree
items.blurb: A cafe in town with a food zone, drinks and a chill rooftop. There's a food and dessert menu — order iced milk and snacks for kids while the adults sip coffee. Open all day.

items.name: Som tam & laap (order for the adults)
items.blurb: Bold local dishes the adults shouldn't miss — fiery Sisaket-style som tam and local laap and koi. Order a separate plate for kids, and you can ask the shop to make it mildly spicy if you want the kids to try it.

items.name: Sweets & snacks at the evening market
items.blurb: The evening market in town has plenty of sweets and snacks — Thai desserts, fried bites, cut fruit — so kids can walk around and sample several things in one place. Cheap.

items: Accommodation, 1 night — a mid-range hotel in town with a family room runs about 800–1,500 THB; guesthouses start around 400–800 THB. Choosing somewhere in town makes it easier to get around with kids.

Entry fees — Sisaket Aquarium is 30 THB for adults, 20 for kids (children under 100 cm free); Huai Nam Kham island, the Million Bottle Temple and Phra That Rueang Rong are free. Check the water park's fee on its page before going.
Car — renting and driving yourself runs about 1,000–1,500 THB a day plus fuel, worth it if you have kids and plan to head south.
Food, 2 days — local food, in-town shops, cafes and markets run about 1,000–1,500 THB for a family of four for the whole trip.
Souvenirs / fruit — volcanic durian (in season), rambutan, mangosteen, jasmine rice, dyed fabric — optional extras as you like.

blocks.text: When is the best time to take kids to Sisaket

blocks.html: If you want your kids to eat volcanic durian and fresh orchard fruit, come around mid June–August. Late June is peak, and there's usually a volcanic durian festival in Kantharalak. If fruit isn't the point, the cool season around November–January is comfortable for keeping kids outdoors longer. The Isan sun is strong almost year-round, so take kids out in the morning or late afternoon for the most comfort, and avoid 12:00–15:00 when it's harshest. Bring hats, drinking water and sunscreen for the kids.

blocks.title: What to know about the Khao Phra Wihan–Pha Mo I Daeng border area
blocks.html: If you're thinking of going on to Pha Mo I Daeng or Khao Phra Wihan, I'll be straight with you: Pha Mo I Daeng in Khao Phra Wihan National Park was announced temporarily closed to tourism from 29 May 2025 due to tension along the Thai–Cambodian border, with no firm reopening date. With kids you need to be even more careful — always check the park's latest announcement and border news before planning. If it's still closed, don't try to enter. The family plan above doesn't rely on this spot anyway, so you can drop it without losing the trip.

blocks.title: What to pack before heading out with kids
blocks.html: Bring drinking water, hats, kids' sunscreen, mosquito repellent and snacks for the car, since some stretches drive far before you reach a shop. Wear comfortable walking shoes. At the Million Bottle Temple or the island where there's water nearby, keep kids close. Pack a spare set of clothes if you'll swim or visit the water park, and check the aquarium's opening times before going, since it's closed on Mondays.

faq.q: Where should I take kids in Sisaket?
faq.a: Kids' favorite is Sisaket Aquarium, with its underwater glass tunnel and a diver fish-feeding show. Next is Huai Nam Kham island, where they can cycle and run around; the Million Bottle Temple, which is colorful and fun for photos; and during June–August, the volcanic durian orchards where you can sit and eat fruit in the grove. None of it is far apart.

faq.q: What time does Sisaket Aquarium open, and how much is entry?
faq.a: It's open Tuesday–Sunday, 10:00–16:00, closed every Monday. Entry is 30 THB for adults, 20 THB for kids; children under 100 cm tall, seniors aged 60 and over, and monks enter free. Every day at 14:00 there's a diver fish-feeding show in the big tank that kids love. It's on Huai Nam Kham island in town.

faq.q: Where is the Million Bottle Temple, and can kids visit?
faq.a: The Million Bottle Temple (Wat Pa Maha Chedi Kaew) is in Non Sung subdistrict, Khun Han district, about 1–1.5 hours from town. It's decorated with over 1.5 million colored glass bottles, which kids love for the bold colors and oddity. Open around 08:00–17:00, free entry; dress modestly in the hall area. There's an ordination hall over water, so keep a close eye on kids near it.

faq.q: When can I take kids to eat volcanic durian straight from the orchard?
faq.a: Volcanic durian season runs roughly mid June to August, peaking in late June, when there's usually a volcanic durian festival in Kantharalak. Many orchards around Khun Han–Bak Dong let you sit and eat in the grove, with rambutan and mangosteen for kids too. Prices at the orchard run about 180–250 THB/kg. It's busy at peak, so you can book an orchard ahead; out of season most orchards close.

faq.q: Do I need a car to travel Sisaket with kids?
faq.a: The family-friendly sights in town are close enough that you can call a ride, but if you want to head south to the Million Bottle Temple, the durian orchards or the waterfalls around Khun Han–Kantharalak, about 1–1.5 hours from town, public transport is very limited. I'd rent a car and drive yourself — it's more flexible with kids, and you can stop for the bathroom and rest whenever your little one needs it.
